N_10.answer_text: Aegeon is sentenced to death because he is a Syracusian merchant who has been found in Ephesus, which is forbidden by law due to longstanding enmity between the two cities. Duke Solinus explains that "it hath in solemn synods been decreed / Both by the Syracusians and ourselves, / To admit no traffic to our adverse towns" and that "if any Syracusian born / Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies, / His goods confiscate to the duke's dispose, / Unless a thousand marks be levied, / To quit the penalty and to ransom him" [C2]. Aegeon's entire substance is valued at less than a hundred marks, making him unable to pay the required ransom [C2]. The Duke later grants him one day to "seek thy life by beneficial help: / Try all the friends thou hast in Ephesus; / Beg thou, or borrow, to make up the sum, / And live; if no, then thou art doom'd to die" [C10].

Aegeon traveled to Ephesus because he was "coasting homeward" after spending five summers searching "furthest Greece" and "the bounds of Asia," and though he was "hopeless to find" his lost family, he was "loath to leave unsought / Or that or any place that harbours men" [C10].

Based on Aegeon's account, the shipwreck separated the family when their vessel struck a mighty rock and split in two. Aegeon had fastened himself to one mast with one of his twin sons and one of the twin servants (Dromio), while his wife had fastened herself to another mast with the other twin son and the other twin servant [C6]. When the ship broke apart, "in this unjust divorce of us, Fortune had left to both of us alike what to delight in, what to sorrow for" [C8]. Aegeon's wife's portion, carrying her and the two children with her, was driven faster by the wind and was rescued by fishermen of Corinth [C8]. Aegeon's portion was later picked up by a different ship from Epidaurus, whose crew would have taken the wife and children from the Corinthian fishermen had their boat not been too slow [C8]. Thus, the family was divided into two groups, each believing the other lost.

Earlier, in [C38], Antipholus of Syracuse states he gave gold to Dromio (his own servant, Dromio of Syracuse) which is "laid up Safe at the Centaur," but notes "I could not speak with Dromio since at first I sent him from the mart." 

Later, in [C129], when Dromio of Syracuse arrives with gold saying "Master, here's the gold you sent me for," Antipholus of Syracuse responds confusedly, "What gold is this?" [C129]. This confusion stems from Antipholus of Syracuse interacting with the wrong Dromio in [C16], leading him to believe his own servant failed to safeguard or deliver the money as instructed.
